The logbook of Lighthouse Keeper #0 did not begin with "Day 1." It began with a single, jagged scratch across the first page, followed by the words: *I do not remember arriving.*

Elias Thorne was not his real name, though he had worn it for so long that the shape of it felt like skin. He was simply Keeper #0. The designation was stenciled in faded white paint above the heavy iron door of the lantern room, visible only to those who had climbed the two hundred and fourteen steps from the sea level below. There was no Keeper #1. There had never been a Keeper #2. There was only Elias, and the light.

The lighthouse stood on a jagged tooth of granite known as The Needle, three miles off the coast of a country that no longer appeared on modern maps. To reach it, one had to sail through waters so black they seemed to absorb the stars. The supply boat came once every six months, weather permitting. It dropped crates of tinned beef, salted pork, kerosene, and books. It never took anyone away. Elias had tried to flag them down three times in his memory. He had waved a red handkerchief until his arm burned with lactic acid. The boat had always turned back into the fog before it reached the rocks.

Elias did not mind the isolation. In fact, he preferred it. The silence of The Needle was not empty; it was heavy, thick like wool, pressing against his eardrums. It was a silence that allowed him to hear the ocean breathing.

The fog did not roll in; it descended, heavy and suffocating, like a wet wool blanket pulled tight over the world. It erased the horizon, swallowed the sea, and turned the air into a gray soup where sound traveled strangely—muffled, distant, or deceptively close.

Elias Thorne was Keeper #1 of the Blackrock Point Lighthouse. He was not the only keeper, technically; there had been others before him, and there would be others after him. But for Elias, who had held the post for thirty-two years, he was simply *the* keeper. The number was a bureaucratic artifact, a designation on a manifest that meant nothing to the salt-crusted reality of his life. Here, at the edge of the continent, where the Atlantic gnawed relentlessly at the granite foundations, there was only one man and one light.

His day began not with an alarm, but with the rhythm of the mechanism itself. The lens rotated every fifteen seconds, a slow, hypnotic sweep that painted the darkness with a blade of white fire. Elias watched it from the gallery, his hands wrapped around a mug of coffee that had gone lukewarm hours ago. He didn’t drink it; he held it for the warmth, a small anchor in the cold void.

He was sixty-four years old, though the sea aged men differently. His face was a map of weathered leather, deep lines carved by wind and squinted eyes. The logbook entry for October 14th was brief, written in a hand that had grown shaky with age and the tremors of isolation: *"Wind from the southwest. Visibility poor. The fog does not roll in; it rises from the water like breath. Keeper #2 reports all systems nominal."*

Elias Thorne was Keeper #2. He did not remember being Keeper #1, nor did he recall the transition. In the grand, dusty archives of the Maritime Bureau, records were often fragmented by fire, flood, or simple bureaucratic neglect. But on the jagged spit of rock known as Blackwood Point, there was only one man, one light, and an endless, churning gray expanse of ocean.

Elias had arrived at Blackwood Point during a storm so violent it seemed to tear the sky open. He remembered the smell of ozone and salt, the scream of the wind against the lantern glass, and then… silence. When he woke, the storm had passed, leaving behind a world stripped of color. The sun, when it rose, looked pale and sickly, like a bruised fruit.

He was not alone in his duty, though he spoke to no one. Every day, just before dusk, a small wooden rowboat would appear from the mist, carrying supplies: tinned food, kerosene, spare wicks, and letters that were never addressed to him but always found their way into his pocket. These letters contained cryptic instructions—*Check the third gear on the rotation mechanism.* *Listen for the bell at midnight.* *Do not look directly into the sea when it turns black.*
